Does subroutines give us advantages in code merklization (giving nice boundaries for chunking code)? i agree, and we can work on improving the process later - but i feel like we should address the feedback first I think previously <@273808422753796097> indicated that code merklization works "well enough" by just doing `n` byte chunks without any need to actually understand the code layout, but I may be mis-remembering. might open door for a subroutine-based merkleization approach. but since historical contracts don't have subroutines we can't really run the numbers on that approach. The fixed size chunk approach is generally believed simple-and-good-enough wouldn't it make it trickier since you can jump to the middle of a subroutine? If someone is jumping into the middle of a subroutine they can suffer with poor gas costs. 🙂 Or is jumping to the middle of a subroutine supposed to be a standard practice? if jumping into subroutines become disallowed that needs some special handling yeah i don't think it reasonably possible to disallow something like that since it would be expensive to validate Is it worth opening the discussion of dropping 2315 from Berlin? The fact that the solidity team strongly opposes it concerns me. I would hate to have an EIP that doesn't properly serve their needs since their compiler generates more EVM bytecode than any other tool and they probably have the best insight into the EIP's usefulness. *solidity developer (I don't think we should be assigning the views of an individual to the views of the team they represent without evidence of such) agreed, but i'm going off this comment from `@ekpyron` and `@ethchris`'s tweet I *suspect* that the consensus will be to not pull it, but it may be worth having them bring their concerns to an ACD meeting to see if there is interest in a last minute removal consideration. unfortunately neither of them are in this discord to discuss 😖 why are people arguing against EIPs via Twitter? I'm a VERY STRONG 👎 on any code merklization approaches that are tied to EVM semantics. The bytecode should be opaque bytes. Otherwise we bind the EVM semantics to the merklization scheme and end up with some really costly interdependencies somewhere down the line.... The savings at the witness and networking level are not nearly enough (IMHO) to justify the complexity As an engineer who has, on occasion, found themselves having to read bytecode or decompiled bytecode, I would appreciate higher level structures in the bytecode itself. Reading CLR and Java bytecode, for example, is *way* easier than reading x86 bytecode. This isn't a strong argument to add these features to the EVM, but it does make me appreciate the value a bit and why static analyzers would prefer it. It's worth pointing out that 2315 was a stripped down version of <@!683653554631868440>'s first EIP for subroutines, 615. I suspect that _if_ we were to remove 2315 to do a "more complete version", we'd likely end up back at something that looks like 615 and the solution we took there was 2315. I also see that this EIP (https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2327) is being proposed for London, which takes some stuff out of 615 as well. 2315 should be submitted for Review status by the way (all Berlin EIPs should be review). I have a number of editorial points of feedback that won't be surfaced until that happens. Is ACD too late to make this decision? With the ropsten fork block approaching rapidly, i'm afraid there will be even less desire to remove it on friday Is it a security issue? I think the argument is that it is an EIP which arguably adds little/no value and introduces technical debt. (not my position, summary of how I understand the opposition) But I think this is maybe _by design_, given we did not do EIP-615 but did this one instead. Have we disabled/broken dynamic jumps yet? For example, I suspect we'll get similar pushback if we do "BLS but Eth2 support only" Ah, I see, this EIP is one step toward getting rid of dynamic jumps. I'm a fan of that end goal. Might be worth mentioning that 2315 is a step toward 615 in the 2315 discussion thread. End goal is good, but in this specific case the argument "lets drip it in bit by bit" does not really work really well. Because it is likely by the time other pieces are considered "ready", we will realise that we should have done this first piece differently 😦 Therefore I was arguing from the start for either including something like 615 as whole, but not piece by piece I'm a fan of breaking up into multiple EIPs as was done. I would not be opposed to all of those EIPs landing together though. at this point, we can "wait and see" but also in this specific case, I think this EIP is not very harmful, so far it looks to me that it might be reasonably compatible with the future pieces the "nasty" edge cases are mostly related to when `JUMP` or `JUMPI` go into the middle of subroutine. Hopefully at the end of the road, when these two opcodes are eventually disabled, these edge cases will disappear BTW, I am sure it was discussed before, but I don't find this case in the EIP, what should happen if there is `JUMPDEST` inside the subroutine and we jump into it, and then hit `RETURNSUB` without having ever done `JUMPSUB` ? ah, ok, it is shallow return stack, sorry ok, I think I am cool with EIP 🙂 I object very strongly to reopening discussion on EIP-2315. It's has already been discussed and agreed to on the appropriate forums. For over a year now. The EIP-615 proposal from which it came has been discussed for over five years. It feels like it has been agreed to out of attrition of critics, rather than proponents who plan to use the EIP once it is deployed. I find it very concerning that several members of the Solidity team oppose the EIP, as I would expect an EIP like this should most directly benefit them. The team did not oppose the proposal in the end, stated that they could use it for calling Solidity functions, and made a preliminary implementation in Yul. I'm referring to Chris' tweet yesterday and `@ekpyron` post on the FEM thread earlier today, where he says specifically that he feels like this EIP should not have been accepted into Berlin due to the lack of practical uses They are free to express their opinions. Can you share where the solidity team backed 2315? If that is the case, then I am happy to drop this. I don't have time to review the entire thread. At this point it is up to the critics to convince the core devs to abandon the EIP. It is not my job to go back to January of 2020 and start to defend it all over again. It's scheduled for Berlin. Yes, exactly this Especially with Verkle trees/Kate, thanks to which the penalty for proofs needing to access a bunch of disparate chunks of the code will drop to zero Agreed, and I'm not asking you to defend it. I will continue looking, but I do not see where the Solidity team has backed 2315. My general philosophy here is that I would like ethereum state (including accounts, code chunks and storage) to operate on an abstraction layer above a single key/value tree. Because this minimizes client code complexity, and makes it easier to upgrade the tree structure (eg. to STARK witnesses once we need post-quantum) in the future So basically Ethereum state storage systems should not ever need to know anything about *what* it is storing? right, exactly The Solidity team has generally not sent a representative to ACD calls. I don't know why not. But therefore they never participated in the final consensus to include it. I agree this is unfortunate. If they oppose it now the appropriate course of action is to place an item on the Agenda for the ACD call and send a representative. And key/value store is the most general-purpose standard that you can get. We are likely to announce the upgrade and communicate the client releases tomorrow or Thursday. I think if core devs want to see this removed, we greatly minimize disruption by agreeing to this now vs. on the call. Ropsten is scheduled to fork in just over a week, so there is a pretty high cost to changing things now, and even more so after the client versions have been announced.
